arXiv:2610.24897v1 [cs.LG] 17 Oct 2026

Distribution-based regularization for reward fine-tuning diffusion and flow models

Romeo Passaro∗,1,2 Jeongjae Lee∗,3,4,5 Jong Chul Ye3 Michael M. Bronstein1,2
Yoshua Bengio4,5 Alexander Tong2,† Danyal Rehman2,4,5,†
1University of Oxford  2AITHYRA  3KAIST  4Mila – Québec AI Institute  5Université de Montréal
*Equal contribution; ordering determined by a random draw.   †Corresponding authors
Abstract

Reward fine-tuning is an effective way to adapt pretrained diffusion and flow-matching models to downstream objectives, but aggressive optimization often leads to mode collapse and distributional drift. Existing methods attempt to control this drift with reverse-KL regularization, implemented as an ℓ2\ell_{2} penalty on the velocity field; however, this functions by indirectly constraining sampling dynamics rather than directly acting on the generated distribution. To address this, we propose DFR (Distributional Functional Rewards), which augments the task reward with a distribution-dependent, per-sample reward that acts explicitly on the generated distribution. Formally, we generalize the KL-regularized objective from expected rewards, which are linear in the model’s distribution, to convex functionals of it. The first variation of this objective defines an effective, distribution-dependent reward that directly penalizes deviation from the pretrained distribution. This formulation yields additive per-sample rewards for the Fréchet distance (FD), maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), and DreamSim diversity, recovering several recently proposed rewards as special cases. Across various text-to-image fine-tuning tasks, DFR matches the peak reward of KL-tuned baselines while increasing diversity by up to 29% at equal or lower drift.

Code: https://github.com/jaylee2000/dfr

1 Introduction

Diffusion and flow-matching models (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021; Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Albergo et al., 2023; Peluchetti, 2023) have become a dominant paradigm for generative modeling across various data modalities, including images (Rombach et al., 2022; Labs et al., 2025), videos (Wan et al., 2025), and molecular structures (Abramson et al., 2024). These models learn stochastic or deterministic dynamics that transport a simple source distribution to a complex target distribution. However, downstream applications rarely value all samples equally: the goal is often to shift probability mass toward high-reward samples, while preserving the diversity and capabilities of the pretrained model. Reward fine-tuning achieves this by adapting the pretrained model toward a downstream reward (Uehara et al., 2024).

For non-differentiable rewards, existing approaches broadly fall into two families: (1) Trajectory-based methods, which formulate sampling as a multi-step Markov decision process (MDP), treating each step of the sampling process as an action (Black et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2023); and (2) ELBO-based methods, which instead treat the final sample as the action and approximate its intractable log-likelihood with an evidence lower bound (McAllister et al., 2026). Recently, ELBO-based methods have emerged as particularly attractive options for large-scale text-to-image fine-tuning, reporting up to ∼50×\sim 50\times faster training than trajectory-based methods at comparable reward and image quality (Zheng et al., 2026; Xue et al., 2026; Bergmeister et al., 2026).

Across both families, however, reward maximization alone does not specify which properties of the pretrained distribution ought to be preserved. In particular, optimizing toward increasingly high-reward samples can reduce sample diversity and move the generated distribution away from the pretrained model. Existing methods often address this tension through KL regularization, typically implemented as an ℓ2\ell_{2} penalty between the fine-tuned and pretrained velocity fields (Fan et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025b). However, this regularization acts on the model’s sampling dynamics, whereas the properties of ultimate interest—diversity and retention of the pretrained distribution—are properties of its output distribution. This raises the natural question:

We answer this question affirmatively with Distributional Functional Rewards (DFR), a general framework for distribution-regularized reward fine-tuning. DFR unifies trajectory- and ELBO-based methods by augmenting reward optimization with objectives defined directly on the generated distribution. This allows models to improve reward while better preserving the pretrained distribution. Our main contributions are:

  • •

    A unified framework for distribution-regularized reward fine-tuning. DFR generalizes KL-regularized reward optimization to convex functionals of the clean-sample distribution, including maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), Fréchet distance (FD), and diversity objectives. Their first variations induce distribution-dependent per-sample reward corrections, enabling direct control of the generated distribution in both trajectory- and ELBO-based methods.

  • •

    Improved distribution preservation at matched reward. On GenEval and OCR with SD3.5-M, DFR reduces drift from the pretrained model by up to 12% and increases diversity by up to 29% relative to KL-regularized baselines at matched reward, while training 36–41×\times faster than Flow-GRPO.

  • •

    Compatibility with both feature- and latent-space objectives. We instantiate DFR with feature-space objectives such as FD and DreamSim diversity, as well as latent-space MMD, demonstrating strong performance even without the use of pretrained feature encoders.

  • •

    Minimal overhead over KL-regularized fine-tuning. Compared with KL-tuned RAM, DFR adds little training cost: DFR-MMD reaches GenEval 0.95 with only 7% more training time than RAM (β=\beta= 3) while achieving 9% higher diversity, and DFR-DS reaches OCR 0.96 with only 1% more time than RAM (β=\beta= 5) while achieving 17% higher diversity.

2 Background

2.1 Flow-Based Models

Flow-based models—including diffusion and flow-matching frameworks (Lipman et al., 2023; Song et al., 2021)—learn a time-dependent velocity field vθ​(𝒙t,t){{v}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t},t) that transports samples between a source distribution, typically Gaussian noise ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), and the data distribution 𝒙0∼pdata{\bm{x}}_{0}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}. For the commonly used linear path 𝒙t=(1−t)​𝒙0+t​ϵ{\bm{x}}_{t}=(1-t){\bm{x}}_{0}+t\boldsymbol{\epsilon}, the corresponding target velocity is simply 𝒙˙t=ϵ−𝒙0\dot{{\bm{x}}}_{t}=\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-{\bm{x}}_{0}. The velocity field is therefore learned by weighted regression toward this target:

ℒFM​(θ)=𝔼t,𝒙0,ϵ​[w⁡(t)​‖vθ​(𝒙t,t)−(ϵ−𝒙0)‖22],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t,{\bm{x}}_{0},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\left[w(t)\left\|{{v}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t},t)-(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-{\bm{x}}_{0})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right], (1)

where w⁡(t)>0w(t)>0 is a timestep-dependent weighting function. At inference, samples are generated by drawing ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) and integrating the learned dynamics backward from t=1t=1 to t=0t=0. We denote the frozen pretrained velocity field by vref{{v}}_{\text{ref}} and the endpoint distribution induced by vθ{{v}}_{\theta} under the chosen sampler by pθ​(𝒙0)p_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{0}), omitting conditioning for brevity. This integration takes the form of an SDE for diffusion models and an ODE for flow-matching models; we refer the reader to Tong et al. (2023); Liu et al. (2025b) for a more detailed equivalence between the two formulations.

2.2 Reward fine-tuning via policy gradients

Reward fine-tuning adapts a pretrained generative model to a downstream reward while regularizing deviations from the pretrained distribution.11 1 See Uehara et al. (2025) for a review of inference-time reward alignment. This is most often formulated as KL-regularized reward maximization:

maxθ𝔼𝒙0∼pθ[r(𝒙0)]−β𝒟KL(pθ(𝒙0)∥pref(𝒙0)),\max_{\theta}\;\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}_{0}\sim p_{\theta}}[r({\bm{x}}_{0})]-\beta\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(p_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{0})\,\|\,p_{\text{ref}}({\bm{x}}_{0})\right), (2)

where β>0\beta>0 controls the reverse-KL regularization strength, and pθp_{\theta} and prefp_{\mathrm{ref}} are the endpoint distributions of the fine-tuned and pretrained models, respectively. For non-differentiable rewards, the gradient of the expected rewards can be evaluated using the REINFORCE identity (Williams, 1992):

∇θ𝔼𝒙0∼pθ​[r⁡(𝒙0)]=𝔼𝒙0∼pθ​[(r⁡(𝒙0)−b)​∇θ​log⁡pθ​(𝒙0)],\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}_{0}\sim p_{\theta}}[r({\bm{x}}_{0})]=\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}_{0}\sim p_{\theta}}\left[(r({\bm{x}}_{0})-b)\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{0})\right], (3)

where bb is a sample-independent baseline used to reduce variance, and the difference r⁡(𝒙0)−br({\bm{x}}_{0})-b defines the advantage. In practice, advantages are often normalized within groups of samples from the same prompt (Shao et al., 2024), while clipped likelihood ratios can further stabilize training optimization (Schulman et al., 2017).

For flow-based models, however, the marginal log-likelihood log⁡pθ​(𝒙0)\log p_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{0}) is intractable. Trajectory-based methods replace it with the per-step transition likelihoods of a stochastic sampler. ELBO-based methods instead replace it with −ℒFM​(θ,𝒙0)-\mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}}(\theta;{\bm{x}}_{0}), the loss of Eq. (1) evaluated on a single generated sample. For suitable w⁡(t)w(t), this is an evidence lower bound up to an additive constant (McAllister et al., 2026; Choi et al., 2026). Substituting it into Eq. (3) gives online reward-weighted regression (RWR): the model is trained with the flow-matching loss on its own samples, each weighted by its advantage (Fan et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2026). We build on RAM (Bergmeister et al., 2026), which takes this form. See Appendix B for a detailed derivation of these equivalences.

Regularization. While trajectory- and ELBO-based methods differ in how they estimate the reward gradient, both typically approximate the reverse-KL term in Eq. (2) using a squared velocity anchor:

ℒanchor​(θ)=𝔼⁡[‖vθ​(𝒙t,t)−vref​(𝒙t,t)‖22].\mathcal{L}_{\text{anchor}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|{{v}}_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{t},t)-{{v}}_{\text{ref}}({\bm{x}}_{t},t)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]. (4)

For Gaussian transition kernels, a time-weighted form of Eq. (4) equals the KL divergence between the path distributions of the fine-tuned and pretrained samplers, which upper-bounds the reverse-KL divergence of Eq. (2) (Fan et al., 2023, Equation 7).

2.3 Distributional Measures

Fréchet distance (FD). For a feature encoder ϕ\phi, let μp\mu_{p} and Σp\Sigma_{p} denote the mean and covariance of ϕ⁡(𝒙)\phi({\bm{x}}) under 𝒙∼p{\bm{x}}\sim p. The Fréchet distance (FD) compares the first two feature moments of pp and qq:

FD⁡(p,q)≜‖μp−μq‖22+tr⁡(Σp+Σq−2​(Σq1/2​Σp​Σq1/2)1/2).\mathrm{FD}(p,q)\triangleq\|\mu_{p}-\mu_{q}\|_{2}^{2}+\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\Sigma_{p}+\Sigma_{q}-2\bigl(\Sigma_{q}^{1/2}\Sigma_{p}\Sigma_{q}^{1/2}\bigr)^{1/2}\right). (5)

Maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) is a classical kernel two-sample discrepancy (Gretton et al., 2006). For a chosen kernel k⁡(⋅,⋅)k(\cdot,\cdot),

MMDk2​(p,q)=𝔼𝒙,𝒙′∼p​[k⁡(𝒙,𝒙′)]+𝔼𝒚,𝒚′∼q​[k⁡(𝒚,𝒚′)]−2​𝔼𝒙∼p𝒚∼q​[k⁡(𝒙,𝒚)],\mathrm{MMD}_{k}^{2}(p,q)=\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}},{\bm{x}}^{\prime}\sim p}[k({\bm{x}},{\bm{x}}^{\prime})]+\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{y}},{\bm{y}}^{\prime}\sim q}[k({\bm{y}},{\bm{y}}^{\prime})]-2\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\bm{x}}\sim p\\ {\bm{y}}\sim q\end{subarray}}[k({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})], (6)

where a characteristic kernel ensures MMDk​(p,q)=0\mathrm{MMD}_{k}(p,q)=0 if and only if p=qp=q. Note, MMD\mathrm{MMD} requires no feature encoder and can be computed directly in latent space.

DreamSim diversity. DreamSim (Fu et al., 2023) is a perceptual distance trained to align with human judgments of visual similarity. Given the normalized DreamSim feature z⁡(𝒙)=ϕDS​(𝒙)/‖ϕDS​(𝒙)‖2z({\bm{x}})=\phi_{\mathrm{DS}}({\bm{x}})/\|\phi_{\mathrm{DS}}({\bm{x}})\|_{2}, DreamSim diversity (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025) is the mean pairwise cosine distance between independent samples, which equals the total variance of the normalized features:

DivDS​(p)=𝔼𝒙,𝒙′∼p​[1−z​(𝒙)⊤​z​(𝒙′)]=1−‖𝔼𝒙∼p​[z⁡(𝒙)]‖22=tr⁡Cov𝒙∼p​[z⁡(𝒙)].\mathrm{Div}_{\mathrm{DS}}(p)=\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}},{\bm{x}}^{\prime}\sim p}\bigl[1-z({\bm{x}})^{\top}z({\bm{x}}^{\prime})\bigr]=1-\bigl\|\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}\sim p}[z({\bm{x}})]\bigr\|_{2}^{2}=\operatorname{tr}\,\mathrm{Cov}_{{\bm{x}}\sim p}[z({\bm{x}})]. (7)

3 DFR: Distributional Regularization for Reward Fine-Tuning

The velocity anchor in Eq. (4) only indirectly controls the reverse-KL divergence in Eq. (2), as it penalizes changes in the sampling dynamics even when the endpoint distribution pθp_{\theta} is unchanged. In ELBO-based methods, heuristic time weighting at forward-noised states further weakens this correspondence. We nevertheless retain the velocity anchor for training stability and to limit drift, yet we complement it with a term that acts directly on the generated distribution. Importantly, the two objectives are compatible: the optimal fine-tuned process preserves the pretrained model’s conditional noising process (demonstrated in Appendix C.2).

We generalize the KL-regularized objective of Eq. (2) from expected rewards to convex functionals of the generated distribution (Section 3.1). The first variation of such a functional acts as a per-sample reward, which any policy gradient method can optimize without further changes (Section 3.2), and instantiate the framework with MMD, FD, and DreamSim diversity (Section 3.3).

3.1 Distributional regularization through convex functionals

Let ℱ:𝒫⁡(𝒳)→ℝ\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be a convex functional of the generated distribution. Consider the entropy-regularized optimization problem

p⋆=arg​minp∈𝒫⁡(𝒳)(ℱ(p)+β𝒟KL(p∥pref)),β>0.p^{\star}=\argmin_{p\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X})}\left(\mathcal{F}(p)+\beta\,\mathcal{D}_{\text{KL}}(p\|p_{\text{ref}})\right),\qquad\beta>0. (8)

For a signed measure η\eta on 𝒳\mathcal{X} with η⁡(𝒳)=0\eta(\mathcal{X})=0, the first-order change of ℱ\mathcal{F} along η\eta defines the functional derivative δ​ℱδ​p​(p,⋅):𝒳→ℝ\frac{\delta\mathcal{F}}{\delta p}(p,\cdot):\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} through

limε→0ℱ⁡(p+ε​η)−ℱ⁡(p)ε≜∫δ​ℱδ​p​(p,𝒙)​η​(𝑑𝒙).\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{\mathcal{F}(p+\varepsilon\eta)-\mathcal{F}(p)}{\varepsilon}\triangleq\int\frac{\delta\mathcal{F}}{\delta p}(p,{\bm{x}})\,\eta(\mathrm{d}{\bm{x}}). (9)

Since η\eta integrates to zero, δ​ℱδ​p\frac{\delta\mathcal{F}}{\delta p} is defined only up to an additive constant. Under standard regularity and integrability assumptions, this (strictly) convex minimization problem has a unique minimum. Standard variational calculus techniques identify the unique minimizer with the following equation:

p⋆​(𝒙)=1Z⁡(p⋆)​pref​(𝒙)​exp⁡(−1β​δ​ℱδ​p​(p⋆,𝒙)),p^{\star}({\bm{x}})=\frac{1}{Z(p^{\star})}\,p_{\text{ref}}({\bm{x}})\exp\left(-\frac{1}{\beta}\frac{\delta\mathcal{F}}{\delta p}(p^{\star},{\bm{x}})\right), (10)

where Z⁡(p⋆)Z(p^{\star}) is the normalizing constant. Eq. (10) is generally an implicit fixed point condition because the functional derivative may itself depend on p⋆p^{\star}. We refer the reader to Hu et al. (2021) for a formal treatment of this problem, and to Appendix C.1 for a looser derivation. We apply this result to two choices of ℱ\mathcal{F}: the expected reward, and the expected reward with a convex distributional penalty.

Expected rewards as the linear case. Standard expected reward maximization, Eq. (2), corresponds to ℱ⁡(p)=−𝔼𝒙∼p​[r⁡(𝒙)]\mathcal{F}(p)=-\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}\sim p}[r({\bm{x}})], which is linear in pp with first variation −r⁡(𝒙)-r({\bm{x}}). Eq. (10) then reduces to the familiar exponential tilt:

p⋆​(𝒙)=1Z​pref​(𝒙)​exp⁡(r⁡(𝒙)β),p^{\star}({\bm{x}})=\frac{1}{Z}\,p_{\text{ref}}({\bm{x}})\exp\left(\frac{r({\bm{x}})}{\beta}\right), (11)

whose right-hand side has no dependence on p⋆p^{\star}.

Distribution-level effective reward. Distributionally regularized reward maximization corresponds to

ℱ⁡(p)=−𝔼𝒙∼p​[r⁡(𝒙)]+λ​ℛ​(p),λ≥0,\mathcal{F}(p)=-\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}\sim p}[r({\bm{x}})]+\lambda\,\mathcal{R}(p),\qquad\lambda\geq 0, (12)

where ℛ⁡(p)\mathcal{R}(p) is a convex functional that measures how far pp is from prefp_{\text{ref}}. For brevity, we omit its dependence on the fixed prefp_{\text{ref}}. This ℱ\mathcal{F} is no longer linear but remains convex in pp, with first variation

δ​ℱδ​p​(p,𝒙)=−r⁡(𝒙)+λ​δ​ℛδ​p​(p,𝒙),\frac{\delta\mathcal{F}}{\delta p}(p,{\bm{x}})=-r({\bm{x}})+\lambda\,\frac{\delta\mathcal{R}}{\delta p}(p,{\bm{x}}), (13)

which, unlike in the linear case, depends on pp. We call its negative the effective reward22 2 Here and below, the argument after the semicolon is the distribution at which the derivative is taken, and 𝒙{\bm{x}} is the sample at which it is evaluated. For example, ℛ⁡(p)=12​‖𝔼𝒙∼p​[z⁡(𝒙)]‖22\mathcal{R}(p)=\tfrac{1}{2}\|\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}\sim p}[z({\bm{x}})]\|_{2}^{2} gives rℛ​(𝒙,p)=−z​(𝒙)⊤​𝔼𝒙′∼p​[z⁡(𝒙′)]r_{\mathcal{R}}({\bm{x}};p)=-z({\bm{x}})^{\top}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}^{\prime}\sim p}[z({\bm{x}}^{\prime})].:

reff​(𝒙,p)≜r⁡(𝒙)+λ​rℛ​(𝒙,p),rℛ​(𝒙,p)≜−δ​ℛδ​p​(p,𝒙).r_{\text{eff}}({\bm{x}};p)\triangleq r({\bm{x}})+\lambda\,r_{\mathcal{R}}({\bm{x}};p),\qquad r_{\mathcal{R}}({\bm{x}};p)\triangleq-\frac{\delta\mathcal{R}}{\delta p}(p,{\bm{x}}). (14)

Substituting Eq. (14) into Eq. (10) gives

p⋆​(𝒙)=1Z⁡(p⋆)​pref​(𝒙)​exp⁡(reff​(𝒙,p⋆)β).p^{\star}({\bm{x}})=\frac{1}{Z(p^{\star})}\,p_{\text{ref}}({\bm{x}})\exp\left(\frac{r_{\text{eff}}({\bm{x}};p^{\star})}{\beta}\right). (15)

This is the exponential tilt of Eq. (11) with rr replaced by reffr_{\text{eff}}, so the penalty acts exactly like an additional reward. Unlike Eq. (11), it cannot be evaluated directly, because reffr_{\text{eff}} depends on the unknown p⋆p^{\star}. We therefore approach p⋆p^{\star} by gradient descent, evaluating reffr_{\text{eff}} at the current model instead.

3.2 Optimizing distributional functionals via policy gradients

We minimize ℱ⁡(pθ)\mathcal{F}(p_{\theta}) over the generator parameters θ\theta; the reverse-KL term of Eq. (8) is handled separately below. An infinitesimal change in θ\theta perturbs the distribution in the direction η=∇θpθ\eta=\nabla_{\theta}p_{\theta}, which has zero total mass, so the definition in Eq. (9) gives the chain rule

∇θℱ​(pθ)=∫δ​ℱδ​p​(pθ,𝒙)​∇θpθ​(𝒙)​𝑑𝒙.\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{F}(p_{\theta})=\int\frac{\delta\mathcal{F}}{\delta p}(p_{\theta},{\bm{x}})\,\nabla_{\theta}p_{\theta}({\bm{x}})\,\mathrm{d}{\bm{x}}. (16)

Using ∇θpθ=pθ​∇θ​log⁡pθ\nabla_{\theta}p_{\theta}=p_{\theta}\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta} and Eq. (14),

−∇θℱ​(pθ)=𝔼𝒙∼pθ​[reff​(𝒙,pθ)​∇θ​log⁡pθ​(𝒙)].-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{F}(p_{\theta})=\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}\sim p_{\theta}}\left[r_{\text{eff}}({\bm{x}};p_{\theta})\,\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}({\bm{x}})\right]. (17)

This is the REINFORCE identity of Eq. (3) with reffr_{\text{eff}} in place of rr. As in the ordinary chain rule, the derivative is evaluated at the current pθp_{\theta} and is not itself differentiated: reff​(𝒙,pθ)r_{\text{eff}}({\bm{x}};p_{\theta}) is a scalar weight attached to each sample, and no gradient flows through ℛ\mathcal{R} or any feature extractor it uses.

In practice, we draw a group of samples from pθp_{\theta}, estimate rℛ​(𝒙i,pθ)r_{\mathcal{R}}({\bm{x}}^{i};p_{\theta}) for each sample from the statistics of that group (denoted p^\hat{p}), and add λ​rℛ\lambda\,r_{\mathcal{R}} to the sample’s advantage (Algorithm 1, shaded line). Since 𝔼𝒙∼pθ​[∇θ​log​pθ​(𝒙)]=0\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}\sim p_{\theta}}[\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}({\bm{x}})]=0, adding a constant to reffr_{\text{eff}} leaves the gradient unchanged; the additive constant left free in Eq. (9) is the baseline bb of Eq. (3), which is why we may center rℛr_{\mathcal{R}} within each group.

Application to flow models. We use RAM (Bergmeister et al., 2026), the state-of-the-art ELBO-based method, as our base framework. The score in Eq. (17) is replaced by the ELBO surrogate −∇θℒFM​(θ,𝒙)-\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta;{\bm{x}}) alluded to in Eq. (1), and the reverse-KL term in Eq. (8) by ℒanchor​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\text{anchor}}(\theta) (Eq. (4)). The complete training pipeline is provided in Algorithm 1.

Algorithm 1 implements the population formulation with three finite-sample choices. All quantities are conditional: ℛ\mathcal{R} is applied to pθ(⋅∣𝒄)p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid{\bm{c}}) and averaged over conditions 𝒄{\bm{c}}, which we omit for brevity. The distributional reward is centered within each group and added to the normalized task advantage rather than to rr before normalization; the two differ only in the rescaling of λ\lambda by the advantage scale. The population statistics entering rℛr_{\mathcal{R}} are estimated from the group of GG samples for MMD and DreamSim diversity, excluding the sample itself from pairwise averages, and from an exponential moving average of feature moments pooled over prompts for FD (detailed in Appendix C.6.3).

3.3 Instantiations: MMD, FD, Dreamsim Diversity

We instantiate ℛ\mathcal{R} with three functionals: (1) the MMD reward, our primary choice, which requires no pretrained encoder; (2) the FD reward; and (3) the DreamSim reward. The latter two show that DFR subsumes recently proposed diversity and FD-based rewards as special cases; Section 4 evaluates all three under the same protocol. All three functionals are convex in pp (Appendix C.4), so the analysis in Section 3.1 applies directly (for FD, see the remark in Appendix C.6.3).

MMD reward. Let ψ:𝒳→ℝm\psi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{m} be a fixed injective map and b∈(0,2)b\in(0,2), and define

ρb​(𝒙,𝒚)=‖ψ⁡(𝒙)−ψ⁡(𝒚)‖2b.\rho_{b}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})=\|\psi({\bm{x}})-\psi({\bm{y}})\|_{2}^{b}. (18)

We use the identity map for ψ\psi, meaning ρb\rho_{b} reduces to a power of the Euclidean distance in latent space and requires no pretrained encoder, although an encoder could be used instead. The corresponding MMD can be written as

MMDkb2⁡(p,pref)\displaystyle\operatorname{MMD}_{k_{b}}^{2}(p,p_{\text{ref}}) =𝔼𝒙∼p𝒚∼pref​[ρb​(𝒙,𝒚)]−12​𝔼𝒙,𝒙′∼p​[ρb​(𝒙,𝒙′)]−12​𝔼𝒚,𝒚′∼pref​[ρb​(𝒚,𝒚′)].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\bm{x}}\sim p\\ {\bm{y}}\sim p_{\text{ref}}\end{subarray}}\left[\rho_{b}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})\right]-\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}},{\bm{x}}^{\prime}\sim p}\left[\rho_{b}({\bm{x}},{\bm{x}}^{\prime})\right]-\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{y}},{\bm{y}}^{\prime}\sim p_{\text{ref}}}\left[\rho_{b}({\bm{y}},{\bm{y}}^{\prime})\right]. (19)

The proof is in Appendix C.3. Consider the MMD functional ℛMMD​(p,pref)=MMDkb2⁡(p,pref)\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{MMD}}(p,p_{\text{ref}})=\operatorname{MMD}_{k_{b}}^{2}(p,p_{\text{ref}}).

Proposition 1 (MMD reward).

A representative of the negative functional derivative of ℛMMD\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{MMD}} is

rMMD​(𝒙,p,pref)=𝔼𝒙′∼p​[ρb​(𝒙,𝒙′)]−𝔼𝒚∼pref​[ρb​(𝒙,𝒚)].\boxed{r_{\mathrm{MMD}}({\bm{x}};p,p_{\text{ref}})=\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}^{\prime}\sim p}\left[\rho_{b}({\bm{x}},{\bm{x}}^{\prime})\right]-\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{y}}\sim p_{\text{ref}}}\left[\rho_{b}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})\right].} (20)

The proof is given in Appendix C.5. The two terms in Eq. (20) have complementary roles. The first is a repulsive term that rewards samples far from other samples generated by the current model, thereby discouraging collapse. The second is an attractive term that penalizes samples far from the pretrained distribution, thereby limiting distributional drift.

FD reward. DFR also recovers FD-based reward augmentation. With μp,Σp\mu_{p},\Sigma_{p} as in Section 2.3, consider the FD functional ℛFD​(p)=FD⁡(p,pref)\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{FD}}(p)=\mathrm{FD}(p,p_{\text{ref}}) of Eq. (5).

Proposition 2 (FD reward).

Assume the covariance matrices are positive definite and define

Gp=I−Σq1/2(Σq1/2ΣpΣq1/2)−1/2Σq1/2G_{p}=I-\Sigma_{q}^{1/2}\left(\Sigma_{q}^{1/2}\Sigma_{p}\Sigma_{q}^{1/2}\right)^{-1/2}\Sigma_{q}^{1/2} (21)

for q≡prefq\equiv p_{\text{ref}}. A representative of the negative functional derivative of ℛFD\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{FD}} is

rFD​(𝒙,p)=−[2​(μp−μq)⊤​f+(f−μp)⊤​Gp​(f−μp)].\boxed{r_{\mathrm{FD}}({\bm{x}};p)=-\left[2(\mu_{p}-\mu_{q})^{\top}f+(f-\mu_{p})^{\top}G_{p}(f-\mu_{p})\right].} (22)

The proof is given in Appendix C.6. The two terms in Eq. (22) have complementary roles. The first penalizes shifts in the population feature mean, while the second corrects changes in feature covariance.

DreamSim diversity reward. DFR also recovers pairwise perceptual diversity rewards. With z⁡(𝒙)z({\bm{x}}) defined in Section 2.3, the cosine similarity between two samples is z​(𝒙)⊤​z​(𝒙′)z({\bm{x}})^{\top}z({\bm{x}}^{\prime}). We consider the population-average cosine-similarity functional ℛDS​(p)=12​(1−DivDS​(p))\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{DS}}(p)=\frac{1}{2}(1-\mathrm{Div}_{\mathrm{DS}}(p)) of Eq. (7).

Proposition 3 (DreamSim reward).

A representative of the negative functional derivative of ℛDS\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{DS}} is

rDS​(𝒙,p)=−z​(𝒙)⊤​𝔼𝒙′∼p​[z⁡(𝒙′)].\boxed{r_{\mathrm{DS}}({\bm{x}};p)=-z({\bm{x}})^{\top}\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}^{\prime}\sim p}[z({\bm{x}}^{\prime})].} (23)

The proof is given in Appendix C.7.

4 Experiments

We evaluate whether DFR improves the trade-off between reward and reward hacking beyond what tuning the reverse-KL coefficient of the baseline can achieve.

4.1 Setup

Tasks and methods. We fine-tune Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium (SD3.5-M; Esser et al., 2024) on two tasks: (1) Compositional generation (GenEval; Ghosh et al., 2023), with reward thresholds 0.95 and 0.96, and (2) Visual text rendering (OCR), with threshold 0.96. We adopt RAM (Bergmeister et al., 2026) as the ELBO-based framework on which DFR builds on. We sweep its reverse-KL coefficient β\beta over {1,…,4}\{1,\dots,4\} for GenEval and {2,…,6}\{2,\dots,6\} for OCR. DFR-MMD, DFR-FD, and DFR-DS augment RAM with the distributional rewards introduced in Section 3.3 (Algorithm 1). For each variant, we use the largest β\beta for which RAM reaches the highest reward threshold, or the next smaller value when the distributional reward itself provides substantial regularization toward the pretrained model. All configurations are trained with three random seeds under identical compute budgets.

Baselines. We compare DFR against other ELBO- and trajectory-based methods including DiffusionNFT (Zheng et al., 2026), AWM (Xue et al., 2026), RSM (Lee et al., 2026), and Flow-GRPO (Liu et al., 2025b) on both the compositional generation and visual text rendering tasks.

Protocol. Because reward hacking intensifies over the course of optimization, we compare models at matched target reward levels. For each seed, we evaluate the first checkpoint that reaches a given threshold; a configuration is considered to reach that threshold only if all three seeds do so.

Metrics. Following Liu et al. (2025d); Liu et al. (2025c); Domingo-Enrich et al. (2025), we measure reward hacking by drift and diversity, each computed per-prompt over 64 images. Drift is the Fréchet distance to the 64 images of prefp_{\text{ref}} in Inception-v3 and DINOv2 features. Diversity is measured by DreamSim diversity, computed with its DINO and OpenCLIP branches. Preference rewards such as ImageReward (Xu et al., 2023) and PickScore (Kirstain et al., 2023) are reported but not used, since they score each image in isolation and cannot detect a model that generates near-identical images for every seed. Two configurations are tied on a metric if their means differ by at most the larger of their standard deviations; otherwise, the configuration with the better mean wins. Entries computed with an encoder that a DFR instance uses in its reward, or a closely related one, are counted as neither wins nor losses. Consequently, the main text reports the OpenCLIP branch, which no instance trains on. Additional training, evaluation, and baseline details are provided in Appendix D.

4.2 Results

DFR moves beyond the β\beta trade-off. Every DFR instance lies beyond RAM’s β\beta path, with less drift and/or more diversity (Figure 2). Further, DFR also wins or ties against all RAM configurations that reaches the same threshold on every drift and diversity metric (Tables 1 and 2). The gap is widest at the highest threshold, GenEval 0.96: among RAM configurations only β=\beta= 2 reaches it, whereas all three DFR instances do, with lower drift (FID 111–114 vs. 120) and higher diversity (0.193–0.225 vs. 0.174). On OCR, DFR-MMD and DFR-FD drift the least, and DFR-DS is the most diverse.

The instances behave as their rewards predict. The DreamSim reward is purely repulsive, whereas MMD and FD rewards also pull samples toward prefp_{\text{ref}} (Section 3.3). Accordingly, on every task and threshold, DFR-DS attains the highest diversity of the three instances but the smallest reduction in drift, while DFR-MMD and DFR-FD reduce drift the most. On OCR, for example, DFR-DS matches RAM (β=5\beta=5) in FID (136 vs. 137), while raising diversity by 17%, whereas DFR-MMD and DFR-FD lower FID to 121–125 despite running at the smaller β=4\beta=4. The attractive term also acts as additional regularization: on OCR, DFR-DS trains as fast as RAM at the same β\beta, whereas DFR-MMD and DFR-FD require a smaller β\beta to reach the threshold and still take longer.

DFR-MMD matches DFR-FD without an encoder. DFR-MMD computes its reward on SD3.5-M’s own VAE latents with eight reference samples per prompt, whereas DFR-FD relies on three pretrained encoders, precomputed reference statistics, and a per-encoder calibration. Despite this, DFR-MMD ties DFR-FD on every drift metric at every threshold, matches its diversity on GenEval, and reaches the thresholds at least as fast, although it is less diverse on OCR (0.197 vs. 0.213).

DFR adds modest cost. Distributional rewards add only 3–9% to the time per training step. Reaching a threshold takes longer than RAM at the same β\beta, but the cost is comparable to that of reducing drift by raising β\beta. Image quality and prompt generalization are also preserved: ImageReward and PickScore remain comparable to those of the RAM configurations that reach the same threshold.

5 Related Work

Regularization for reward fine-tuning. Most reward fine-tuning methods for flow-based models use the velocity anchor in Eq. (4), which constrains the sampling dynamics rather than pθp_{\theta} itself (Section 3.1). DDRL (Ye et al., 2025) instead regularizes toward an off-policy data distribution using the forward-KL divergence, implemented through an ELBO objective on real data or pretrained-model samples. Flow Density Control (De Santi et al., 2025) also optimizes functionals of the generated distribution, using gradients of the effective reward. DFR instead uses the effective reward only as a scalar signal in policy-gradient updates, without differentiating through it, which makes it directly applicable to non-differentiable rewards, and we provide extensive empirical evidence of scalability through systematic experiments on SD3.5-M.

Diversity and distributional rewards.Objectives defined as functionals of a distribution have been studied in reinforcement learning (Hazan et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020). Several works augment the target reward with diversity or distributional signals. GARDO (He et al., 2025) increases the rewards of high-quality samples far from their nearest neighbors, while DiverseGRPO (Liu et al., 2025a) assigns bonuses based on semantic-cluster sizes; neither signal is derived from an explicit distributional objective. DRIFT (Liu et al., 2026) rewards each sample by its mean squared DreamSim distance to the other samples in its group, which coincides with the DreamSim instance of DFR (see Appendix C.7).

Other methods match a prescribed target distribution. LOO-FID (Baran et al., 2026) and Miao et al. (2024) reward samples by their leave-one-out change in, respectively, the FD to real-image statistics and the MMD to curated reference images; these are finite-difference estimates of the corresponding first variations (Appendix C.6.2). kCGM (Diamant and Trippe, 2026) minimizes MMD to a target feature distribution using an estimator of the form in Eq. (16). DistWise (Li et al., 2026) uses the FID between a large generated set and real data as a distribution-level reward, while DRAGON (Bai et al., 2025) contrasts positive and negative generation sets under distribution-level rewards. In these methods, matching a real or curated target distribution—typically in a pretrained feature space—is itself the objective. By contrast, DFR derives per-sample rewards as first variations of convex functionals of pθp_{\theta}, yielding the explicit objective in Eq. (12), where deviation from the pretrained model distribution regularizes target-reward maximization alongside the KL anchor. Consequently, DFR requires neither an image dataset nor, for its MMD instance, a pretrained encoder.

6 Conclusion

In this work, we introduce Distributional Functional Rewards (DFR), a general-purpose framework for reward fine-tuning that complements KL regularization with objectives defined directly on the model’s output distribution. By deriving per-sample rewards from the first variations of distributional functionals, DFR provides explicit control over diversity and distributional drift. Our findings clearly demonstrate that KL regularization has a limited effective range: beyond it, stronger regularization slows optimization, limits reward improvement, and/or destabilizes training. On two distinct tasks: compositional generation and visual text rendering, we find that DFR consistently improves the reward–distribution trade-off beyond what is attainable by tuning the KL coefficient alone. At matched task reward, every evaluated DFR variant improves diversity, reduces drift, or both, while matching or improving all eligible distributional metrics relative to KL-only RAM baselines that reach the same reward threshold. These gains require only a simple reward augmentation, adding 3–9% overhead per training step, while not relying on a pretrained encoder. Overall, DFR enables reward fine-tuning to achieve high task rewards, while better preserving diversity and remaining closer to the pretrained model distribution than KL regularization alone.

Limitations and future work. Although presented as a general-purpose reward fine-tuning framework, our experiments are focused on validation in image settings; extending DFR to other modalities such as video and molecular structures is a natural next step to more effectively evaluate the generalization of the framework. Further, since the distributional reward regularizes toward prefp_{\text{ref}}, it preserves the pretrained model’s biases along with its diversity, so its coefficient λ\lambda must be tuned jointly with β\beta. Balancing DFR’s repulsive and attractive terms more carefully is a promising direction for improving this trade-off. Our characterization of the optimum assumes exact optimization of the population objective, which the ELBO surrogate and the finite-sample estimates of the distributional rewards approximate in practice.

Appendix A Extended Related Work

Differentiable rewards. When the reward is differentiable, its gradient can be propagated directly through the generative process. DRaFT (Clark et al., 2024) backpropagates through the sampling chain, optionally truncating the gradient to the final steps, whereas ReFL (Xu et al., 2023) backpropagates through a single late denoising step from which the clean sample is predicted directly. Adjoint Matching (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025) formulates fine-tuning as stochastic optimal control under a memoryless noise schedule, whose optimum solves Eq. (2), and regresses the velocity toward a target defined by an adjoint state that propagates the reward gradient backward along the trajectory. Shin et al. (2026) reduce its cost using a linear base drift, enabling few-step deterministic sampling and a closed-form adjoint. VGG-Flow (Liu et al., 2025c) matches the difference between fine-tuned and pretrained velocities to the gradient of a learned value function, while ∇\nabla-GFlowNet (Liu et al., 2025d) derives gradient-informed GFlowNet objectives; both seek to preserve the pretrained prior and sample diversity. For broader unifying perspectives on reward fine-tuning, we refer readers to Uehara et al. (2024); Choi et al. (2026); Lee et al. (2026); Xu et al. (2026).

Non-differentiable rewards. Trajectory-based methods formulate denoising as a multi-step MDP and apply policy gradients to per-step transition likelihoods (Black et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025b; Xue et al., 2025). Because these likelihoods require stochastic transitions, the sampling ODE is converted to an SDE with the same marginals. Li et al. (2025); He et al. (2026) improve efficiency by restricting stochastic sampling and optimization to a subset of timesteps.

ELBO-based methods instead treat the final sample as a single action and replace its intractable log-likelihood log⁡pθ​(𝒙0)\log p_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{0}) with the ELBO surrogate −ℒFM​(θ)-\mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}}(\theta), producing an online reward-weighted regression objective on forward-noised samples (McAllister et al., 2026; Fan et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2026). Although this gives a biased estimator of the exact policy gradient, it is empirically effective. Methods derived from other perspectives reduce to the same objective (Zheng et al., 2026; Bergmeister et al., 2026); Appendix B gives these reductions in a common notation. By decoupling optimization from sampling, ELBO-based methods can substantially accelerate reward maximization relative to trajectory-based methods (Choi et al., 2026).

Distributional discrepancies as training losses. Several few-step distillation methods match the output distribution of a student generator to that of a pretrained teacher, through the integral reverse-KL divergence (Luo et al., 2024; Yin et al., 2024b; Yin et al., 2024a), general ff-divergences (Xu et al., 2025), or moment matching (Salimans et al., 2024). Other works match the data distribution directly. Zhou et al. (2025) train few-step generators from scratch with an MMD-based moment-matching objective, and De Bortoli et al. (2025) learn the full conditional distribution of clean data given a noisy state with scoring rules such as the energy score, rather than regressing its mean. FD-loss (Yang et al., 2026) post-trains generators by minimizing the Fréchet distance to real data in a representation space.

A.1 Measuring fidelity and diversity

Distribution-level fidelity. FID (Heusel et al., 2017) compares generated and real images through the Fréchet distance between Gaussian fits to their Inception-v3 features. Its limitations have motivated several alternatives. Stein et al. (2023) find that Inception features align poorly with human judgments of modern generators and recommend DINOv2 features instead. KID (Bińkowski et al., 2018) and CMMD (Jayasumana et al., 2024) replace FD with MMD, which drops the Gaussian assumption and admits an unbiased estimator. Precision and recall (Kynkäänniemi et al., 2019) separate fidelity from coverage by estimating the support of each distribution with kk-nearest-neighbor balls in feature space.

Diversity. LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018) and DreamSim (Fu et al., 2023) compare images through deep features calibrated to human similarity judgments. LPIPS mainly reflects low-level differences such as color and texture, whereas DreamSim also captures layout, pose, and semantic content. The mean pairwise perceptual distance within a set of samples is a common diversity measure in reward fine-tuning (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025d; Liu et al., 2025c). The Vendi Score (Friedman and Dieng, 2023) instead measures the effective number of distinct samples, as the exponential of the entropy of the eigenvalues of the normalized similarity matrix.

Appendix B Unifying online RWR

Several recent ELBO-based methods have different motivations, but their updates reduce to the same online reward-weighted regression (RWR) objective (Lee et al., 2026; Kveton et al., 2026; Choi et al., 2026). This appendix derives the reduction for ORW-CFM-W2, FPO, AWM, RAM, DiffusionNFT, and AdvantageFlow, and summarizes it in Table 3.

Notation. We translate every method into the conventions of Section 2.1 and Algorithm 1. Time t=0t=0 is clean data and t=1t=1 is noise 33 3 ORW-CFM-W2 and FPO denote clean data at time 11; we substitute t↦1−tt\mapsto 1-t. , with 𝒙t=(1−t)​𝒙0+t​ϵ{\bm{x}}_{t}=(1-t)\,{\bm{x}}_{0}+t\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}, ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), and vfwd=ϵ−𝒙0{{v}}_{\text{fwd}}=\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-{\bm{x}}_{0} . We write vθ{{v}}_{\theta}, vold{{v}}_{\text{old}}, and vref{{v}}_{\text{ref}} for the velocities of the current, lagged, and pretrained models, all evaluated at (𝒙t,t)({\bm{x}}_{t},t), and omit conditioning. Rollouts are drawn as 𝒙0∼pθold{\bm{x}}_{0}\sim p_{\theta_{\text{old}}}, with θold=θ\theta_{\text{old}}=\theta for on-policy methods, and timesteps are sampled from a distribution p⁡(t)p(t), i.e., t∼p⁡(t)t\sim p(t). As in the main text, β\beta is the coefficient of the anchor to vref{{v}}_{\text{ref}}; we write γ\gamma for the coefficient of the anchor to vold{{v}}_{\text{old}}. The reward enters through a scalar weight f⁡(r⁡(𝒙0),t)f(r({\bm{x}}_{0}),t). For most methods f=A⁡(𝒙0)/αf=A({\bm{x}}_{0})/\alpha, where AA is the group-normalized advantage and 1/α1/\alpha a reward coefficient; for ORW-CFM-W2, f=exp⁡(r⁡(𝒙0)/α)f=\exp(r({\bm{x}}_{0})/\alpha).

Unified gradient. Setting aside clipping and loss transformations, which we discuss for each method, every method below updates θ\theta along

g⁡(θ)\displaystyle g(\theta) =𝔼t,𝒙0,ϵ​[2​(∇θvθ)⊤​(β⁡(vθ−vref)⏟ref. anchor+γ⁡(vθ−vold)⏟old anchor+f⁡(r⁡(𝒙0),t)​(v∙−vfwd)⏟RWR)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{t,{\bm{x}}_{0},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\Big[2(\nabla_{\theta}{{v}}_{\theta})^{\top}\Big(\underbrace{\beta\,({{v}}_{\theta}-{{v}}_{\text{ref}})}_{\text{ref.\ anchor}}+\underbrace{\gamma\,({{v}}_{\theta}-{{v}}_{\text{old}})}_{\text{old anchor}}+\underbrace{f(r({\bm{x}}_{0}),t)\,({{v}}_{\bullet}-{{v}}_{\text{fwd}})}_{\text{RWR}}\Big)\Big], (24)

where the sampling distribution of 𝒙0{\bm{x}}_{0} is held fixed when differentiating. Eq. (24) is exactly the gradient of the regression loss

𝔼t,𝒙0,ϵ​‖vθ−sg⁡[vθ+β⁡(vref−vθ)+γ⁡(vold−vθ)+f⁡(r⁡(𝒙0),t)​(vfwd−v∙)]‖22,\mathbb{E}_{t,{\bm{x}}_{0},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\Big\|{{v}}_{\theta}-\operatorname{sg}\!\Big[{{v}}_{\theta}+\beta\,({{v}}_{\text{ref}}-{{v}}_{\theta})+\gamma\,({{v}}_{\text{old}}-{{v}}_{\theta})+f(r({\bm{x}}_{0}),t)\,({{v}}_{\text{fwd}}-{{v}}_{\bullet})\Big]\Big\|_{2}^{2}, (25)

since the stop-gradient leaves only 2​(∇θvθ)⊤​(vθ−sg⁡[⋅])2(\nabla_{\theta}{{v}}_{\theta})^{\top}({{v}}_{\theta}-\operatorname{sg}[\cdot]). For v∙=vθ{{v}}_{\bullet}={{v}}_{\theta} it is also exactly the gradient of the sum of squares 𝔼⁡[f​‖vθ−vfwd‖22+β​‖vθ−vref‖22+γ​‖vθ−vold‖22]\mathbb{E}\bigl[f\,\|{{v}}_{\theta}-{{v}}_{\text{fwd}}\|_{2}^{2}+\beta\|{{v}}_{\theta}-{{v}}_{\text{ref}}\|_{2}^{2}+\gamma\|{{v}}_{\theta}-{{v}}_{\text{old}}\|_{2}^{2}\bigr], in which the weight ff does not depend on θ\theta.

We call two objectives equivalent when their gradients agree up to a positive constant factor, which can be absorbed into the learning rate. A recurring case is several methods that multiply every term of their loss by the same positive time weight w⁡(t)w(t). We absorb this weight into the time distribution, replacing 𝔼t∼p​[w​(t)​h​(t)]\mathbb{E}_{t\sim p}[w(t)\,h(t)] by 𝔼t∼p~​[h​(t)]\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\tilde{p}}[h(t)], where p~​(t)=p​(t)​w​(t)/Z\tilde{p}(t)=p(t)\,w(t)/Z and Z=𝔼t∼p​[w​(t)]Z=\mathbb{E}_{t\sim p}[w(t)]. Since ZZ does not depend on θ\theta, the two are equivalent. Finally, some reductions hold exactly only at θ=θold\theta=\theta_{\text{old}}, i.e., for on-policy updates; these are marked with an asterisk in Table 3.

B.1 ORW-CFM-W2

ORW-CFM-W2 (Fan et al., 2025) minimizes a reward-weighted flow-matching loss plus an anchor to the pretrained velocity (Fan et al., 2025, Equation 10). Their reward weight exp⁡(τ​r)\exp(\tau\,r) and anchor coefficient α\alpha correspond to our f=exp⁡(r⁡(𝒙0)/α)f=\exp(r({\bm{x}}_{0})/\alpha) and β\beta, and rollouts are drawn from the current model, i.e., θold=θ\theta_{\text{old}}=\theta. Their loss is therefore exactly the sum-of-squares form below Eq. (25), with γ=0\gamma=0 and v∙=vθ{{v}}_{\bullet}={{v}}_{\theta} (Table 3).

B.3 AWM

AWM (Xue et al., 2026) uses the same importance ratio and clipping as FPO (Appendix B.6), but with a velocity-prediction loss and an additional anchor to the pretrained model. The regression loss entering the ratio is (Xue et al., 2026, Equation 15)

ℓθ​(t,ϵ)=wAWM​(t)​‖vθ−vfwd‖22,\ell_{\theta}(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon})=w_{\text{AWM}}(t)\,\|{{v}}_{\theta}-{{v}}_{\text{fwd}}\|_{2}^{2}, (29)

averaged over NmcN_{\text{mc}} pairs (ti,ϵi)(t_{i},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{i}), and the anchor is β​wAWM​(t)​‖vθ−vref‖22\beta\,w_{\text{AWM}}(t)\,\|{{v}}_{\theta}-{{v}}_{\text{ref}}\|_{2}^{2}, whose coefficient coincides with our β\beta (Xue et al., 2026, Equations 13 and 16). With PPO clipping, which the paper omits from its algorithm for simplicity but its implementation includes, the full loss is

ℒAWM​(θ)=−min⁡(ρ^θ​A,clip⁡(ρ^θ,1−ξ,1+ξ)​A)+βNmc​∑i=1NmcwAWM​(ti)​‖vθ−vref‖22,\mathcal{L}_{\text{AWM}}(\theta)=-\min\bigl(\hat{\rho}_{\theta}A,\;\operatorname{clip}(\hat{\rho}_{\theta},1-\xi,1+\xi)\,A\bigr)+\frac{\beta}{N_{\text{mc}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{mc}}}w_{\text{AWM}}(t_{i})\,\|{{v}}_{\theta}-{{v}}_{\text{ref}}\|_{2}^{2}, (30)

with ρ^θ\hat{\rho}_{\theta} as in Eq. (37) and ℓ¯θ\bar{\ell}_{\theta} the average of Eq. (29).

As for FPO, at θ=θold\theta=\theta_{\text{old}} we have ρ^θ=1\hat{\rho}_{\theta}=1, no rollout is clipped, and the ratio term contributes −A​∇θ​log⁡ρ^θ=A​∇θℓ¯θ-A\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\hat{\rho}_{\theta}=A\,\nabla_{\theta}\bar{\ell}_{\theta}. Hence

∇θℒAWM​(θold)=1Nmc​∑i=1Nmc2​wAWM​(ti)​(∇θvθ)⊤​[A⁡(vθ−vfwd)+β⁡(vθ−vref)],\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{AWM}}(\theta_{\text{old}})=\frac{1}{N_{\text{mc}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{mc}}}2\,w_{\text{AWM}}(t_{i})\,(\nabla_{\theta}{{v}}_{\theta})^{\top}\bigl[A\,({{v}}_{\theta}-{{v}}_{\text{fwd}})+\beta\,({{v}}_{\theta}-{{v}}_{\text{ref}})\bigr], (31)

Caveat. In its public implementation44 4 AWM official implementation, AWM replaces the loss inside the ratio, Eq. (29), by a concave transform of the squared error, which it calls a generalized Huber loss:

ℓθ​(t,ϵ)=t⁡[(1D​‖vθ−vfwd‖22+δ)1/2−δ1/2]1/2,δ=10−10,\ell_{\theta}(t,\boldsymbol{\epsilon})=\frac{t\,\Bigl[\bigl(\tfrac{1}{D}\|{{v}}_{\theta}-{{v}}_{\text{fwd}}\|_{2}^{2}+\delta\bigr)^{1/2}-\delta^{1/2}\Bigr]}{1/2},\qquad\delta=10^{-10}, (32)

where DD is the data dimension. This transform is not described in the paper.

B.4 RAM

RAM (Bergmeister et al., 2026) derives its objective from stochastic optimal control (SOC), but approximates the path-cost correction term by zero; this approximation is what reduces the objective to reward-weighted regression. Note that without the correction, the SOC formulation is poorly justified. Therefore, we instead analyze the objective RAM optimizes in practice (Bergmeister et al., 2026, Equation 17),

ℒRAM​(θ)=𝔼t∼p⁡(t),𝒙0∼pθold,ϵ​‖vθ−sg⁡[vref+A⁡(vfwd−vθ)]‖22,p⁡(t)=2​t,\mathcal{L}_{\text{RAM}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t\sim p(t),\,{\bm{x}}_{0}\sim p_{\theta_{\text{old}}},\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\Bigl\|{{v}}_{\theta}-\operatorname{sg}\bigl[{{v}}_{\text{ref}}+A\,({{v}}_{\text{fwd}}-{{v}}_{\theta})\bigr]\Bigr\|_{2}^{2},\qquad p(t)=2t, (33)

where we write AA for the group-normalized advantage that RAM denotes by rr. With β=1\beta=1, the terms vθ{{v}}_{\theta} and −β​vθ-\beta\,{{v}}_{\theta} inside the stop-gradient of Eq. (25) cancel, so Eq. (33) is exactly Eq. (25) with β=1\beta=1, γ=0\gamma=0, f=Af=A, and v∙=vθ{{v}}_{\bullet}={{v}}_{\theta}.

In its implementation, RAM makes two changes: it scales the advantage by a reward coefficient 1/α1/\alpha, and evaluates the velocity inside the RWR term at the lagged parameters, using vold{{v}}_{\text{old}} in place of vθ{{v}}_{\theta}. The implemented loss, 𝔼​‖vθ−sg⁡[vref+Aα​(vfwd−vold)]‖22\mathbb{E}\,\bigl\|{{v}}_{\theta}-\operatorname{sg}\bigl[{{v}}_{\text{ref}}+\tfrac{A}{\alpha}({{v}}_{\text{fwd}}-{{v}}_{\text{old}})\bigr]\bigr\|_{2}^{2}, is therefore Eq. (25) with β=1\beta=1, γ=0\gamma=0, f=A/αf=A/\alpha, and v∙=vold{{v}}_{\bullet}={{v}}_{\text{old}}. Note that this is equivalent to Algorithm 1 with β=1\beta=1 and λ=0\lambda=0.

B.5 DiffusionNFT & AdvantageFlow

DiffusionNFT. With clipped advantage A~=clip⁡(A,−1,1)\tilde{A}=\operatorname{clip}(A,-1,1), the loss is

ℒNFT​(θ)=𝔼t,𝒙0∼pθold,ϵ​[1+A~2​‖(1−ζ)​vold+ζ​vθ−vfwd‖22+1−A~2​‖(1+ζ)​vold−ζ​vθ−vfwd‖22],\mathcal{L}_{\text{NFT}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t,{\bm{x}}_{0}\sim p_{\theta_{\text{old}}},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\Bigl[\tfrac{1+\tilde{A}}{2}\,\bigl\|(1-\zeta)\,{{v}}_{\text{old}}+\zeta\,{{v}}_{\theta}-{{v}}_{\text{fwd}}\bigr\|_{2}^{2}+\tfrac{1-\tilde{A}}{2}\,\bigl\|(1+\zeta)\,{{v}}_{\text{old}}-\zeta\,{{v}}_{\theta}-{{v}}_{\text{fwd}}\bigr\|_{2}^{2}\Bigr], (34)

where we have rewritten their β\beta with ζ(∈{1,0.1})\zeta(\in\{1,0.1\}) (Zheng et al., 2026, Equation 5). Lee et al. (2026, Appendix H.2.1) shows that Eq. (34) is exactly ζ2\zeta^{2} times Eq. (25) with β=0\beta=0, γ=1\gamma=1, f=A~/ζf=\tilde{A}/\zeta, and v∙=vold{{v}}_{\bullet}={{v}}_{\text{old}}, up to a θ\theta-independent constant. Their public implementation additionally adds a small anchor to the pretrained velocity, βNFT​‖vθ−vref‖22\beta_{\text{NFT}}\|{{v}}_{\theta}-{{v}}_{\text{ref}}\|_{2}^{2} with default βNFT=10−4\beta_{\text{NFT}}=10^{-4}, which is not part of the paper; it corresponds to some β>0\beta>0 in Eq. (25), whose exact value depends on the implementation’s loss scaling and on the adaptive weighting discussed below55 5 DiffusionNFT official implementation.

AdvantageFlow (Kveton et al., 2026, Equation 5) states its objective in terms of the clean-sample prediction 𝒙^0=𝒙t−t​v\hat{\bm{x}}_{0}={\bm{x}}_{t}-t\,{{v}}. Since 𝒙^0−𝒙0=t⁡(v−vfwd)\hat{\bm{x}}_{0}-{\bm{x}}_{0}=t\,({{v}}-{{v}}_{\text{fwd}}), every term carries a factor t2t^{2}, which we absorb into the time distribution p⁡(t)p(t). The resulting objective is equivalent to Eq. (25) with f=A~f=\tilde{A} and v∙=vθ{{v}}_{\bullet}={{v}}_{\theta}. AdvantageFlow sets γ\gamma so that the total coefficient A~+γ+β\tilde{A}+\gamma+\beta is positive for every sample, e.g., γ=1.1\gamma=1.1 or γ=1−A~\gamma=1-\tilde{A}, which makes each per-sample loss strictly convex in the prediction (Kveton et al., 2026, Section 3.3).

Caveat. DiffusionNFT replaces the time weighting of the flow-matching loss by an adaptive self-normalization, which it motivates as an alternative to manual tuning of the weighting (Zheng et al., 2026, page 6). Each of the two squared errors in Eq. (34) is divided by the stop-gradient of its mean absolute 𝒙0{\bm{x}}_{0}-prediction error. Since 𝒙^0=𝒙t−t​v\hat{\bm{x}}_{0}={\bm{x}}_{t}-t\,{{v}} gives 𝒙^0−𝒙0=t⁡(v−vfwd)\hat{\bm{x}}_{0}-{\bm{x}}_{0}=t\,({{v}}-{{v}}_{\text{fwd}}), the first and second terms acquire the weights

ω1=tsg⁡(mean⁡|(1−ζ)​vold+ζ​vθ−vfwd|),ω2=tsg⁡(mean⁡|(1+ζ)​vold−ζ​vθ−vfwd|).\omega_{1}=\frac{t}{\operatorname{sg}\bigl(\operatorname{mean}\bigl|(1-\zeta)\,{{v}}_{\text{old}}+\zeta\,{{v}}_{\theta}-{{v}}_{\text{fwd}}\bigr|\bigr)},\qquad\omega_{2}=\frac{t}{\operatorname{sg}\bigl(\operatorname{mean}\bigl|(1+\zeta)\,{{v}}_{\text{old}}-\zeta\,{{v}}_{\theta}-{{v}}_{\text{fwd}}\bigr|\bigr)}. (35)

At θ=θold\theta=\theta_{\text{old}}, both residuals equal vold−vfwd{{v}}_{\text{old}}-{{v}}_{\text{fwd}}, so ω1=ω2\omega_{1}=\omega_{2} and the gradient is that of Eq. (34) multiplied by a per-sample factor. Away from θold\theta_{\text{old}}, however, ω1≠ω2\omega_{1}\neq\omega_{2}, and the two terms no longer combine into Eq. (25). Differentiating the weighted terms directly, the coefficient of the RWR direction vold−vfwd{{v}}_{\text{old}}-{{v}}_{\text{fwd}} becomes

f~=ζ2​[(1+A~)​ω1−(1−A~)​ω2],\tilde{f}=\tfrac{\zeta}{2}\bigl[(1+\tilde{A})\,\omega_{1}-(1-\tilde{A})\,\omega_{2}\bigr], (36)

which is no longer proportional to A~\tilde{A}: a rollout with A~=0\tilde{A}=0 still receives the weight ζ⁡(ω1−ω2)/2\zeta(\omega_{1}-\omega_{2})/2. The adaptive weighting therefore changes the scale and update direction.

B.6 Importance Sampling ratios and clipping

FPO and AWM weight each rollout’s regression loss by an estimated importance ratio and clip it as in PPO (Schulman et al., 2017). We describe the effect for a rollout 𝒙0{\bm{x}}_{0} with advantage AA. Let ℓ¯θ\bar{\ell}_{\theta} be its regression loss averaged over NmcN_{\text{mc}} pairs (ti,ϵi)(t_{i},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{i}), e.g., the average of Eq. (26), and

ρ^θ=exp⁡(−(ℓ¯θ−ℓ¯θold)),ℒ⁡(θ)=−min⁡(ρ^θ​A,clip⁡(ρ^θ,1−ξ,1+ξ)​A).\hat{\rho}_{\theta}=\exp\bigl(-(\bar{\ell}_{\theta}-\bar{\ell}_{\theta_{\text{old}}})\bigr),\qquad\mathcal{L}(\theta)=-\min\bigl(\hat{\rho}_{\theta}A,\;\operatorname{clip}(\hat{\rho}_{\theta},1-\xi,1+\xi)\,A\bigr). (37)

Since ℓ¯θ\bar{\ell}_{\theta} is only an ELBO surrogate for −log⁡pθ​(𝒙0)-\log p_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{0}), up to a θ\theta-independent constant, ρ^θ\hat{\rho}_{\theta} estimates the likelihood ratio pθ​(𝒙0)/pθold​(𝒙0)p_{\theta}({\bm{x}}_{0})/p_{\theta_{\text{old}}}({\bm{x}}_{0}) rather than equaling it.

Clipping. If A>0A>0 and ρ^θ>1+ξ\hat{\rho}_{\theta}>1+\xi, or A<0A<0 and ρ^θ<1−ξ\hat{\rho}_{\theta}<1-\xi, the minimum in Eq. (37) selects the clipped branch, which is constant in θ\theta, and the rollout contributes no gradient. In the other two cases the minimum selects ρ^θ​A\hat{\rho}_{\theta}A. Clipping thus stops updating a rollout once its ratio has moved past 1±ξ1\pm\xi in the direction favored by AA, a trust region around θold\theta_{\text{old}}.

Importance sampling ratio. When the rollout is not clipped, using ∇θρ^θ=ρ^θ​∇θ​log⁡ρ^θ\nabla_{\theta}\hat{\rho}_{\theta}=\hat{\rho}_{\theta}\nabla_{\theta}\log\hat{\rho}_{\theta},

∇θℒ​(θ)=−A​ρ^θ​∇θ​log⁡ρ^θ=ρ^θ​A​∇θℓ¯θ,\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}(\theta)=-A\,\hat{\rho}_{\theta}\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\hat{\rho}_{\theta}=\hat{\rho}_{\theta}\,A\,\nabla_{\theta}\bar{\ell}_{\theta}, (38)

i.e., the RWR gradient A​∇θ​ℓ¯θA\,\nabla_{\theta}\bar{\ell}_{\theta} multiplied by the per-rollout factor ρ^θ\hat{\rho}_{\theta}. At θ=θold\theta=\theta_{\text{old}}, ρ^θ=1\hat{\rho}_{\theta}=1 and no rollout is clipped, which is why the reductions of FPO and AWM hold exactly there. Away from θold\theta_{\text{old}}, the step is reweighted by ρ^θ\hat{\rho}_{\theta} and truncated by clipping, and Eq. (24) captures neither.

Log-ratio surrogate. Huang et al. (2024) show that PPO clipping is a hinge loss on ρ−1\rho-1, and that ρ−1\rho-1 can be replaced by other functions that change sign at ρ=1\rho=1, such as log⁡ρ\log\rho; PCPO (Lee and Ye, 2026) reports that log⁡ρ^\widehat{\log\rho} is a lower-variance estimator than ρ^\hat{\rho} for ρ\rho for diffusion models. Replacing ρ^θ\hat{\rho}_{\theta} by log⁡ρ^θ+1\log\hat{\rho}_{\theta}+1 in Eq. (37) turns the unclipped gradient into −A​∇θ​log⁡ρ^θ=A​∇θℓ¯θ-A\,\nabla_{\theta}\log\hat{\rho}_{\theta}=A\,\nabla_{\theta}\bar{\ell}_{\theta} for every θ\theta, removing the multiplicative factor ρ^θ\hat{\rho}_{\theta}. Clipping log⁡ρ^θ+1\log\hat{\rho}_{\theta}+1 to [1−ξ,1+ξ][1-\xi,1+\xi] is the same as clipping log⁡ρ^θ\log\hat{\rho}_{\theta} to [−ξ,ξ][-\xi,\xi], so the trust region remains.

C.2 Backward consistency.

By the chain rule for relative entropy,

𝒟KL(ℙ∥ℙref)=𝒟KL(ℙ0∥pref)+𝔼x0∼ℙ0[𝒟KL(ℙ(d𝒙1:T∣𝒙0)∥ℙref(d𝒙1:T∣𝒙0))].\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(\mathbb{P}\|\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{ref}}\bigr)=\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(\mathbb{P}_{0}\|p_{\mathrm{ref}}\bigr)+\mathbb{E}_{x_{0}\sim\mathbb{P}_{0}}\left[\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{d}{\bm{x}}_{1:T}\mid{\bm{x}}_{0})\|\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{ref}}(\mathrm{d}{\bm{x}}_{1:T}\mid{\bm{x}}_{0})\right)\right]. (45)

Because ℱ\mathcal{F} depends only on the clean-endpoint marginal, the conditional KL is minimized by

ℙ⋆(d𝒙1:T∣𝒙0)=ℙref(d𝒙1:T∣𝒙0).\mathbb{P}^{\star}(\mathrm{d}{\bm{x}}_{1:T}\mid{\bm{x}}_{0})=\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{ref}}(\mathrm{d}{\bm{x}}_{1:T}\mid{\bm{x}}_{0}). (46)

The optimal process therefore changes the distribution of clean samples, while preserving the pretrained conditional noising process. Equivalently, its backward kernels coincide with those of the pretrained model. This posterior-preservation property was established by Uehara et al. (2024, Theorem 3) and underlies forward-process fine-tuning methods like DiffusionNFT (Zheng et al., 2026).

C.3 Energy distance as an MMD

Following the energy score construction of De Bortoli et al. (2025), we construct the kernel behind ℛMMD\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{MMD}} and show that its squared MMD equals Eq. (19). Let ψ:𝒳→ℝm\psi:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{m} be a fixed injective map and b∈(0,2)b\in(0,2), and define

ρb​(𝒙,𝒚)=‖ψ⁡(𝒙)−ψ⁡(𝒚)‖2b.\rho_{b}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})=\|\psi({\bm{x}})-\psi({\bm{y}})\|_{2}^{b}. (47)

Consider distributions with a finite bb-moment, 𝔼𝒙∼p​‖ψ⁡(𝒙)‖2b<∞\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}\sim p}\|\psi({\bm{x}})\|_{2}^{b}<\infty, so that every expectation of ρb\rho_{b} is finite. The function ρb\rho_{b} is of negative type (Sejdinovic et al., 2013, Proposition 3) and induces the positive definite distance-induced kernel

kb​(𝒙,𝒚)=12​[ρb​(𝒙,𝒙a)+ρb​(𝒚,𝒙a)−ρb​(𝒙,𝒚)],k_{b}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})=\frac{1}{2}\left[\rho_{b}({\bm{x}},{\bm{x}}_{\mathrm{a}})+\rho_{b}({\bm{y}},{\bm{x}}_{\mathrm{a}})-\rho_{b}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})\right], (48)

where 𝒙a∈𝒳{\bm{x}}_{\mathrm{a}}\in\mathcal{X} is an arbitrary anchor (Sejdinovic et al., 2013, Section 4.1). The squared MMD does not depend on the choice of 𝒙a{\bm{x}}_{\mathrm{a}} and equals half of the energy distance (Sejdinovic et al., 2013, Theorem 22), given as Eq. (19).

Second, gg is nondecreasing and concave on positive semidefinite matrices: A↦Σq1/2​A​Σq1/2A\mapsto\Sigma_{q}^{1/2}A\Sigma_{q}^{1/2} is linear and order preserving, the matrix square root is operator monotone and operator concave (Bhatia, 1996, Theorem V.1.9), and the trace is linear and order preserving. using monotonicity with Eq. (62) and then concavity. Thus −2​g​(Σp)-2g(\Sigma_{p}) is convex, and ℛFD\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{FD}} is convex.
